person.name: Lina_Bo_Bardi
person.summary: Lina Bo Bardi was an Italian-born Brazilian architect and designer whose buildings made culture, art, work, and recreation part of shared public life. Her work joined modern construction with Brazilian materials, vernacular forms, and spaces made for everyday use.

conclusion: Lina Bo Bardi's São Paulo Museum of Art continues to exhibit its collection in the building she designed on Avenida Paulista. SESC Pompéia remains a working center for sports, performances, workshops, and leisure in São Paulo. Casa de Vidro is preserved as the Instituto Bardi and presents her home, archive, and work to visitors.

events.title: Birth in Rome
events.description: Achillina Bo is born in Rome to Enrico and Giovanna Bo. She is their oldest child, and Graziella is born later.

events.title: Graduates in Rome
events.description: In 1939, Lina Bo Bardi graduated from the Rome College of Architecture at age 25 with a final project titled The Maternity and Infancy Care Centre. She then moved to Milan and began working with architect Carlo Pagani at Studio Bo e Pagani.

events.title: Opens a Milan Studio
events.description: In 1942, Lina Bo Bardi opens her own architectural studio in Milan. Wartime commissions are scarce. An aerial bombing destroys the office in 1943.

images.caption: Via Gesù, Milan, location of Bo Bardi’s studio
images.creator: Lithobius

events.title: Edits Domus During the War
events.description: From 1944 to 1945, Lina Bo Bardi serves as deputy director of [[Domus|Domus]], an Italian architecture and design magazine, in Milan. In 1945, Domus sends her through war-damaged Italy with Carlo Pagani and photographer Federico Patellani to document the destruction.

Domus.explanation: Founded in Milan in 1928, Domus is an influential Italian magazine about architecture, design, and the visual arts.

events.title: Marries Pietro Maria Bardi
events.description: In 1946, Lina Bo Bardi marries Pietro Maria Bardi in Rome. Pietro Maria Bardi works as an art critic and journalist.

events.title: Moves to Brazil
events.description: In October 1946, Lina Bo Bardi and Pietro Maria Bardi travel from Rome to Rio de Janeiro. The [[Institute of Brazilian Architects]] receives them in Rio.

Institute of Brazilian Architects.explanation: The Institute of Brazilian Architects, known by the Portuguese initials IAB, is a professional association for architects in Brazil.

events.background:
Their participation in the Italian resistance had made postwar life in Italy difficult. Pietro Maria Bardi had already visited Brazil in 1933.

Accounts of where the relocation settled differ. Pietro Maria Bardi’s article places the couple’s permanent move in São Paulo during 1946. Lina Bo Bardi’s article records their arrival in Rio de Janeiro.

events.title: Designs MASP's First Home
events.description: On October 2, 1947, Assis Chateaubriand and Pietro Maria Bardi established the São Paulo Museum of Art (MASP) in São Paulo, with Bardi as its director. Lina Bo Bardi designed the museum's first galleries inside the São Paulo headquarters of the Diários Associados media group.

MASP.explanation: MASP is the common acronym for the São Paulo Museum of Art, a major Brazilian art museum founded in 1947.

Diários Associados.explanation: Diários Associados was a Brazilian media conglomerate founded and directed by Assis Chateaubriand. Its São Paulo headquarters temporarily housed the museum's first offices and galleries.

events.title: Launches Habitat Magazine
events.description: In 1950, Lina Bo Bardi and Pietro Maria Bardi founded Habitat in São Paulo, Brazil. The magazine covered art, architecture, and design, and its title expressed Bo Bardi’s idea of an interior designed to support human life.

events.title: Builds the Glass House
events.description: In 1951, Lina Bo Bardi became a naturalized Brazilian citizen and completed Casa de Vidro in Morumbi, São Paulo. She designed the home for herself and Pietro Maria Bardi as a glass-walled living space raised on slender concrete columns above the wooded site.

images.caption: Casa de Vidro, Lina Bo Bardi’s São Paulo home
images.creator: LeoINN

events.background:
Casa de Vidro stood on a 7,000-square-meter site in the remnants of the Atlantic Forest around São Paulo. It was one of the first three houses in Morumbi. The developer used the completed house to market the neighborhood's remaining lots under the slogan “Architecture and Nature.”

Bo Bardi treated the house as a test of how Italian modernism could work in Brazil. Mies van der Rohe's Farnsworth House and Charles and Ray Eames's Case Study House No. 8 were among the American houses then widely publicized. Bernard Rudofsky's courtyard houses in the Brazil Builds exhibition may also have informed her design. She drew from these examples while seeking a modern architecture connected to local forms and the wooded site.

Thin reinforced-concrete slabs and circular columns carry the main living area above the ground. The columns leave the land and vegetation running beneath it. A courtyard inside the open living space allows trees to grow up from the garden. The dining area, library, and fireplace seating remain open to the forest through the glass walls. Bedrooms occupy the portion of the house set on the hilltop. They face a narrow courtyard beside the staff wing. The kitchen joins the two parts of the plan and included labor-saving devices.

The forest later grew back around the building. It now conceals the house within the wealthy suburb Morumbi became.

events.title: Builds New MASP
events.description: In 1957, Lina Bo Bardi begins the new São Paulo Museum of Art building on Avenida Paulista. Construction is completed in 1968. She displays paintings on glass easels across an open gallery above a public plaza.

images.caption: MASP building on Avenida Paulista, São Paulo
images.creator: Wilfredor

events.background:
Local legislation made the unobstructed view across the site a condition of the commission. Bo Bardi kept the middle of the building open and concentrated its galleries above and below ground level. A 74-meter suspended volume rests on four red concrete columns. Concrete beams run along its length. The structure used raw prestressed concrete without decorative ornament.

Bo Bardi called this approach “Poor Architecture.” She wanted a museum with a simple monumental form. MASP’s collection included works by Bosch, Mantegna, Titian, and Goya. In the gallery, each painting stood on a rough concrete block beneath a glass sheet. The works formed a loose grid without chronological order. Bo Bardi intended the arrangement to disrupt visitors’ expectations of how an art collection should be organized.

events.title: Stages Bahia Exhibition
events.description: In 1959, Lina Bo Bardi and theater director Martim Gonçalves create the Bahia exhibition in São Paulo for the Fifth São Paulo Biennial, an international art exhibition. The exhibition brings artworks, craft objects, music, and photographs from Bahia to Ibirapuera.

events.title: Reclaims Solar do Unhão
events.description: In 1959, Lina Bo Bardi accepts an invitation from Bahia's governor to direct a new art museum in Salvador. She converts Solar do Unhão, a former sugar mill, for the museum. She preserves its colonial exterior and adds a staircase made with traditional materials and abstract geometry.

images.caption: Lina Bo Bardi’s helical staircase at Solar do Unhão
images.creator: Paul R. Burley

events.title: Transforms SESC Pompéia
events.description: In 1977, Lina Bo Bardi began redesigning a former steel drum and refrigerator factory in São Paulo as SESC Pompéia, a leisure center with spaces for sports, workshops, theater, and other activities. After seeing local residents use the site for social gatherings, football, dance, and theater, she preserved the factory sheds and added concrete towers connected by elevated walkways.

images.caption: SESC Pompéia, São Paulo, designed by Lina Bo Bardi
images.creator: paulisson miura from Cuiabá, Brasil

events.background:
SESC was linked to Brazil’s national unions and had been created in the 1940s to provide workers with health services and cultural activities. Bo Bardi called the redevelopment a leisure center. She wanted it to be a place for relaxation and enjoyment. Construction proceeded in stages through 1986.

She exposed the factory’s rough concrete by stripping off old plaster and sandblasting the surfaces. New openings in the walls received bright red sliding screens mounted inside. Her choice of materials gave labor and craftsmanship priority. She believed building work should create jobs for craftspeople and laborers.

The finished complex housed theaters, gymnasiums, a swimming pool, snack bars, leisure areas, restaurants, galleries, and workshops.

events.title: Redesigns Teatro Oficina
events.description: In 1984, Lina Bo Bardi redesigns a burned office building in São Paulo for Teatro Oficina, an experimental theater company. Director Zé Celso commissions the project. She builds the theater largely from painted scaffolding around a narrow stage without conventional seating.

images.caption: Teatro Oficina designed by Lina Bo Bardi
images.creator: Igor Marotti

events.title: Receives São Paulo Survey
events.description: In 1989, the University of São Paulo honored Lina Bo Bardi with the first exhibition of her work. The exhibition took place in São Paulo while she was continuing her architectural work there.

events.title: Dies at Casa de Vidro
events.description: Lina Bo Bardi died at Casa de Vidro in São Paulo, the home she had designed in Morumbi. At her death, she left unfinished designs for a new São Paulo City Hall and a Cultural Center for Vera Cruz.
